provenance: Private Collection, France | | Previously attributed to Antonio Tempesta (1555-1630), as suggested by the later inscription, the present drawing can now be ascribed to Giovanni Guerra. | The elongated figures, the treatment of light and shade using the lighter reserves of the paper, and the theatrical quality of the composition, the present sheet can be compared to the 96 drawings by the artist in Volume 54 (inv. 20773–INV. 20868), now at the Cabinet des Arts Graphiques of the Louvre. The present drawing features the same characters and similar architectural elements as those found in inv. 20802, in the Musée du Louvre. | The numbering in the lower right corner, beneath the drawn frame, appears to be in the same hand as the numbering visible on the sheets from the Louvre album.

title: Saint Matthieu et l'Ange sans cadre | unframed
material: black chalk, pen and brown ink, brown and blue wash, heightened with white, on blue paper
description: Saint Matthieu et l'Ange pierre noire, plume et encre brune, lavis brun et bleu, rehauts de blanc, sur papier bleu, la partie supérieure cintrée black chalk, pen and brown ink, brown and blue wash, heightened with white, on blue paper, shaped top 34 x 18.1cm (13 3/8 x 7 1/8in). sans cadre | unframed
provenance: Count Vilain XIV, Brussels (according to his label '80' see Schwed, 2012) | With Claude van Loock, Brussels, where purchased in 1984 by the present owner | Private Collection, France | | Exhibited | Rennes, musée des Beaux-Arts, Dessins de la collection Christian et Isabelle Adrien, 21 March – 2 August, 2012, no 1 | | Literature | P. Rosenberg et al., Dessins de la collection Christian et Isabelle Adrien, Paris, 2012, no 1 (note by Nicolas Schwed) | | | The present drawing is a study for Ferrari's Saint Matthew, one of the four evangelists which originally hung to the right of the main panel of the polyptych that decorated the high altar of the Church of San Cristoforo in Vercelli. | Gaudenzio Ferrari received the commission for the work on 27 June 1529. As highlighted by Nicolas Schwed (2012), the contract was signed by Gaudenzio in the presence of Giovanni Angelo dei Corradi, Count of Lignana, who represented his young son at the time of signing. The work originally consisted of a polyptych, composed of a central panel, La Madonna degli Aranci, surrounded by four tempera paintings of the evangelists. This configuration followed the Piedmontese tradition of the first half of the 16th century. The drawing, whose contours have been pricked for transfer, shows no compositional differences from the final work. Its highly refined style, the chiaroscuro effect achieved with white gouache, and the angular hands are typical of the artist's studies. The present work can be compared to three drawings- two in the Biblioteca Reale, Turin (inv. nos. 14640 and 16149) and one in the Ambrosiana, Milan (inv. no. 15531).

title: L'Immaculée Conception sans cadre | unframed
description: L'Immaculée Conception porte une inscription 'Dionisio' (en bas au centre) sanguine sur papier, la figure est silhouettée et collé sur une feuille rectangulière bears inscription 'Dionisio' (lower centre) red chalk on paper, cut out and laid down on a rectangular sheet 29.1 x 15.9cm (11 7/16 x 6 1/4in). sans cadre | unframed
provenance: Unidentified mark (L.2882) | The art market, Paris, 1968, where purchased by the present owner | Private Collection, France | | Exhibited | Rennes, musée des Beaux-Arts, Dessins de la collection Christian et Isabelle Adrien, 21 March – 2 August, 2012, no 25 | | Literature | P. Rosenberg et al., Dessins de la collection Christian et Isabelle Adrien, Paris, 2012, no 25 (note by Olivia Savatier Sjöholm) | | This red chalk drawing is a preparatory study for the central group of the altarpiece, originally painted by the young Calvaert for the sacristy of the Church of Santa Lucia, Bologna, where it is mentioned by Francesco Cavazzoni in 1603 in his guide for the city. The work now hangs in the church of Sant'Antonio Abate, Bologna. | A further known preparatory study for the altarpiece, also in red chalk, was sold at Sotheby's, New York on 14 January 1992, lot 21 (previously in the collection of Sir John Witt). In this latter, more finished work, Calvaert has moved the Christ Child to the right of the Virgin, which is where it appears in the finished painting. | The biographer Carlo Cesare Malvasia convincingly dated The Immaculate Conception to Calvaert's early period, an assessment supported by the work's strong stylistic debt to Lorenzo Sabatini (circa 1530–1576). While Sabatini's influence is evident in the altarpiece itself, it is notably absent from the preparatory drawings, which remain highly characteristic of Calvaert's graphic style.

title: Vierge à l'Enfant sans cadre | unframed
material: black and red chalk, heightened with white on paper
description: Vierge à l'Enfant pierre noire et sanguine, rehauts de craie blanche, sur papier black and red chalk, heightened with white on paper 34.2 x 23.9cm (13 7/16 x 9 7/16in). sans cadre | unframed
provenance: Part of the Album Sagredo, his numbering 'B. B. n° : 94' (on the reverse) and 'B.B. n° : 32' (on the mount, lower right) | Doge Nicolò Sagredo, circa 1654 | His brother, Stefano Sagredo, Venice | His nephew, Zaccaria Sagredo (1632-1729), Venice | His wife, Cecilia Sagredo, until her sale in 1743 | Probably Collection John Udny (1727-1800) | Collection Jean-Pierre Cornet, (L. 3507), Paris, circa 1970 (see Ketty Gottardo, 2012) | Sale, Sotheby's, London, 10 December 1975, lot 7 | Sale, Cornette de Saint Cyr, Paris, 20 October 1980, lot 2, where purchased by the present owner | Private Collection, France | | Exhibited | Rennes, musée des Beaux-Arts, Dessins de la collection Christian et Isabelle Adrien, 21 March – 2 August, 2012, no 6 | | Literature | P. Rosenberg et al., Dessins de la collection Christian et Isabelle Adrien, Paris, 2012, no 6 (note by Ketty Gottardo) | | The present study is closely linked to Jacopo Bassano's painting Saint Moro and Saint Roch Adoring the Virgin and Child, now in the Museo Civico, Bassano del Grappa. Characterized by bold strokes in black and red chalk, this drawing belongs to the artist's mature period, around 1576, as noted by Ketty Gottardo (2012). At that time, the Podestà Moro, an emissary of the Serenissima in the Veneto region, commissioned the painting from Bassano in gratitude to the Virgin and Saint Roch for their intervention in the plague that had afflicted the territory. | As Gottardo highlighted in 2012, Bassano's execution of this study reflects his deep indebtedness to his master, Titian. The loose yet dynamic handling of chalk and the rich tonal contrasts evident in the drawing recall Titian's influence. This connection underscores Bassano's synthesis of Venetian colourism with a more vigorous and sculptural approach to form, elements that would become defining features of his mature style. | Two additional preparatory drawings for the Saint Moro and Saint Roch Adoring the Virgin and Child are known, both executed solely in red chalk — a medium rarely used by Bassano. The first appeared on the art market in 1986 and was considered by W. R. Rearick to be an autograph work by Jacopo Bassano. The second, sold in 1992, was attributed by Rearick to Jacopo's son, Leandro Bassano, whom he believed to have collaborated with his father in the execution of the painting. Gottardo rightly observed that while both drawings correspond closely to the handling of the final work, they lack the spontaneity and nuanced play of light and shadow that characterize Jacopo Bassano's works on paper (see W. R. Rearick, 'More Veronese Drawings from the Sagredo Collection', Master Drawings, XXXIII, 1995, 2, pp. 132-143, p. 132; W. R. Rearick, Il disegno veneziano del Cinquecento, Milan 2001, p. 229, note 259). | This group of three drawings may have been part of an album that belonged to the Sagredo family. According to W. R. Rearick, Doge Nicolò Sagredo (1606–1676) was instrumental in forming the Sagredo family collection, laying its foundations in the mid-17th century. Rearick hypothesizes that in 1651, Nicolò Sagredo acquired the majority of the Dal Ponte family's drawing collection. After the Doge's death in 1676, the collection passed to his brother, Stefano Sagredo (1620–1685), and later to his son, Zaccaria Sagredo. A volume containing 201 sheets by Bassano and his school was later acquired in 1762 by John Udny, the British consul in Venice. Given the drawing's stylistic and thematic affinities with other works from the Bassano studio, it is plausible that this sheet was once part of that significant collection.

title: Caprice d'architecture avec figures proche d'une fontaine ; Caprice d'architecture avec dessinateur  (2)
description: Caprice d'architecture avec figures proche d'une fontaine ; Caprice d'architecture avec dessinateur une paire, huile sur toile, ovales a pair, oil on canvas, ovals 130 x 102.5cm (51 3/16 x 40 3/8in). (2)
provenance: With Spiller, London where purchased by the present owner | A distinguished Noble Private Collection, Europe | | The present pair of paintings represent a significant addition to the oeuvre of Francesco Zuccarelli (Pitigliano, 1702-1788 Florence). Whilst we see here the delicate brushwork for which Zuccarelli was well known, these works also represent a slight departure for the artist. Tuscan by birth but adopted by La Serenissima, Zuccarelli has here introduced into his typical rural idyll, depicted in silvery pastel tones, two classical colonnades which guide the eye to the background where he has placed two classical temples. | In contrast to those compositions in which Zuccarelli has paid homage to the architecture of Palladio (see for example F. Spadotto, Francesco Zuccarelli , Milan, 2007, pp. 155-158, cat. nos.109-121; works painted in collaboration with Antonio Visentini (1688-1782), in the present pair, the artist has sought inspiration in Vitruvian treatises. This is evident in his choice of buildings: a temple with a peristyle and a monopteros. Both of these edifices are illustrated in De architectura by Marcus Vitruvius Pollio (1st Century B.C.), translated into Italian and published in Venice in 1556 with illustrations and comments from Andrea Palladio. | The particular revival of the work of the illustrious renaissance architect, Andrea Palladio, was very much promoted by the English Consul to Venice Joseph Smith (1682-1770) and, at this time, saw deeper interest in the earlier architecture in which Andrea Palladio had in turn based his work. | It may even be Consul Smith depicted in the foreground of the second of the two in the present lot, shown seated, studying and sketching the architecture of this golden age but with contemporary, rural life still passing by in the background. | | We are grateful to Dott.ssa Federica Spadotto for her kind help in preparing this catalogue note.

provenance: With Galerie van Diemen, Amsterdam, 1934 | Private Collection, Paris, before 1937 (according to literature) | Sale, Hôtel des Ventes, Martin commissaire – priseur, Versailles, 19 October 1978, lot 12 (as Barend Graat) | With Galerie Marcus, Paris, 1980 | Sale, Drôme Encheres, Valence, 28 February 2019, lot 211, where purchased by the present owner | Private Collection, France | | Literature | E. Plietzsch, 'Jacob Ochtervelt', in Pantheon, vol. 20, 1937, p.368, ill., p. 364 | I. Kunze, 'Depotbilder einer grossen Galerie' in Pantheon, vol. 27, 1941, p. 8. | S. J. Gudlaugsson, 'Representations of Granida in Dutch Seventeenth-Century Painting: III', in Burlington Magazine, vol. 91, 1949, p. 40, fig. 12. | E. Plietzsch, Holländische und Flämische Maler des XVII Jahrhunderts, Leipzig, 1960, p. 64. | R. E. Fleischer, 'Ludolf de Jongh and the Early Work of Pieter de Hooch', in Oud Holland, vol. 92, 1978, p. 53, fig. 9. | S.D. Kuretsky, The Paintings of Jacob Ochtervelt (1634-1682), Oxford, 1979, p. 53, cat. no. 1, fig. 3. | | Gudlaugsson, in her 1949 article, suggests that the painting is inspired by Ludolf de Jongh's Granida and Daifilo, signed and dated 1654, now in Osnabrűck Museum (inv. no L7001, see literature). However in her monograph on the artist, Susan Donahue Kuretsky argues that the present work is stylistically one of Ochtervelt's earliest paintings and dates it to circa 1648-50, when he had just begun his apprenticeship with Nicolaes Berchem. She comments that it is implausible that de Jongh, a more experienced artist, would have borrowed the composition from a younger, less accomplished artist who was at this time, beginning his study; and that, in her opinion, the work is clearly earlier than his Hunters and Shepherds dated 1652, now in Kunstsammlungen Chemnitz, Germany (inv. no. 576) (see: Kuretsky, ibid, p. 53, figs. 4 and 8).

Soubeiran de Pierres, Montpellier before 1927 | Private Collection, France | | The putto at the far left of the present composition is based on the same figure in the Triumph of the Infant Bacchus by Sir Anthony van Dyck (1599-1641), now in the Kunsthaus, Zurich (acc. no. KS 39). The work was likely presented to the artists Cornelis and Lucas de Wael upon Van Dyck's departure from Genoa in 1627 (see S. J. Barnes, Van Dyck. A Complete Catalogue of the Paintings, New Haven 2004, pp. 168-169, no. II.24, ill.). | The authorship of this painting remains a matter of scholarly debate. While some have attributed it to the Genoese artist Andrea Vassallo (active c. 1640), Camillo Manzitti has suggested the Flemish painter Jan Roos (1591-1638). Both of these artists were active in Van Dyck's Genoese circle and engaged in similar mythological compositions. When the work was offered at auction at Anderson Galleries, New York, on the 8 December 1927 (lot 118), it was catalogued as a work by Jakob de Wit (1695–1754), reflecting the fluid nature of its attribution over time.

description: Guirlande de fleurs avec le portrait de la Reine Isabelle II d'Espagne signé 'J. cv k*** fecit' (en bas au centre) et porte une signature et une date 'Gutierrez 1842' (sur le fond du portrait, à droite, partiellement retouchée) huile sur toile signed 'J. cv k*** fecit' (on ledge, lower left, partially strengthened)  and bears signature and date 'Gutierrez 1842' (background of the portrait, right) oil on canvas 85.5 x 66cm (33 11/16 x 26in).
provenance: A distinguished Noble Private Collection, Europe |  | Born in Antwerp, Jan van Kessel was clearly influenced by his grandfather, Jan Brueghel the Elder (1568-1625), a pioneer in the development of garland painting. These paintings, popular during the Counter-Reformation, were typically collaborations between a still life and figure painter, who would contribute the devotional image or portrait in the centre. | It is likely that the present works originally had religious subjects in the centre that were later altered into portraits by Gutierrez de a Vega in the early 19th century.  The sitter in the present work, Isabella II, Queen of Spain (1830- 1904) came to the throne aged 3 upon the death of her father, King Ferdinand VII, who changed the succession laws due to his lack of male heir. A full-length portrait of the sitter by Gutierrez de la Vega was offered at Segre subastas, Madrid, 25 October 2022, lot 121. |  | We are grateful to Dr. Fred Meijer for confirming the attribution on the basis of a colour photograph and for suggesting a date of the 1660s.

In the latter portrait, Princess Augusta-Amèlie, is wearing the exceptional parure which included the 'Leuchtenberg necklace' which she later gifted to her mother-in-law, the Empress Joséphine de Beauharnais (1763-1814).

title: Caprice animé de figures habillées à l'orientale 133.6cm (52 5/8 in). diamètre
description: Caprice animé de figures habillées à l'orientale huile sur toile, tondo oil on canvas, tondo 133.6cm (52 5/8 in). diamètre
provenance: With Spiller, London, where purchased by the present owner | A distinguished Noble Private Collection, Europe | | This hitherto, unpublished painting offers us a fascinating interpretation of the Turkish theme treated by Francesco Zuccarelli (Pitigliano, 1702-1788 Florence). The artist produced a small nucleus of works of 'exotic' subjects, ranging from the Old Testament (such as F. Spadotto, Francesco Zuccarelli , Milan, 2007, cat. nos. 255-257) to the depiction of larger figures in Oriental dress (ibid, cat. nos. 253-254) and the captivating capricci, inspired by the engravings of Robert Wood in his 1753 publication The Ruins of Palmyra, Otherwise Tedmor, in the Desert (op.cit., cat. nos. 413-416). | | In the present Capriccio with figures in Oriental dress, however, Zuccarelli has placed his elegant and refined turbaned figures within a landscape, very Venetian in feel but punctuated with classical ruins designed to pull together the composition. As a whole it shows a happy marriage between the traditional landscapes of the Veneto, for which Zuccarelli was so well known, and elements reflecting the growing fascination with travel literature so resonant of the later 18th century. | | We are grateful to Dott.ssa Federica Spadotto for her kind help in preparing this catalogue note.

title: Allégorie de la vue
description: Allégorie de la vue signé 'Marot/fecit' (en bas à gauche, renforcé) huile sur toile signed 'Marot/fecit' (lower left, strengthened) oil on canvas 83.8 x 126.8cm (33 x 49 15/16in).
provenance: A distinguished Private Collection, Bergerac, where purchased by the present owner | | After training with Charles de La Fosse (1636-1716), François Marot was admitted as a history painter to the Royal Academy of Painting and Sculpture, in Paris, in 1702. He later worked for the King's Buildings and contributed to major commissions, including the History of the King tapestry series (1711) and a painting for the Marble Trianon, Versailles Latona and the Peasants of Lycia (MV 8219 ; B 615) dated 1714 (see F. Marandet, 'Dans le sillage de Charles de La Fosse: François Marot (1666-1719), Les Cahiers d'Histoire de l'Art, 2010, pp. 40-47 and F. Marandet, 'François Marot: quatorze œuvres redécouvertes', Les Cahiers d'Histoire de l'Art, 2015, pp. 68-74). | The present painting, likely part of a series illustrating the five senses, shares key characteristics with an Allegory of Hearing, offered for sale, Semenzato Milan, 19 October 1999, lot 65. Both works share the same dimensions and signature. | Two drawings by Marot confirm the attribution of the painting and shed light on the painting's creation. The first, Study of a figure and putto in a private collection, UK, served as the model for his personification of the figure of the Sight, initially a nude which was then partially draped. The putto's pose was also subtly adjusted to engage the viewer. The second drawing, Study of figure and arms with Galerie Paul Prouté, Paris, may have been drawn in preparation for another allegory from the same series. Notably, it includes two studies of limbs which also relate to the present painting: the raised right hand and the left forearm holding a mirror, which both correspond to the final composition. | | We are grateful to François Marandet for confirming the attribution and for his kind assistance in cataloguing this lot.

title: Etude pour la résurrection du fils de la veuve de Naïm
material: charcoal and white chalk on buff paper
description: Etude pour la résurrection du fils de la veuve de Naïm fusain et craie blanche sur papier beige charcoal and white chalk on buff paper 40.1 x 57.4cm (15 13/16 x 22 5/8in).
provenance: With Jacques Petithory, Paris, where purchased by the present owner in 1969 | Private Collection, France | | This finely executed drawing could possibly be considered a study for Jean-Baptiste Wicar's La Résurrection du fils de la veuve de Naïm, now at the Palais des Beaux-Arts de Lille (P667), a subject drawn from the Gospel of Luke (7:11-17). A key exponent of Neoclassicism, Wicar was deeply influenced by his time in Rome, where he absorbed the academic rigour of the French school while refining his own distinct style. The present sheet showcases his masterful handling of line and composition, with fluid yet precise contours and carefully modulated shading that lend depth and expression to the figures. The dramatic solemnity of the scene, a hallmark of Wicar's historical and religious works, is already palpable in this preparatory stage, offering an insight into his creative process.
